# AICR bundle — Terraform

Generated by AICR v1.0.0.

1 Helm releases, as 1 module calls in `main.tf` —
one per component. A component's pre-manifest, post-manifest and readiness-gate
releases live inside its module, so `depends_on` on the call covers all of them.

## Deploy

This bundle is a **child module**. It has no provider configuration of its own
and no backend: the configuration that calls it owns both.

```hcl
provider "helm" {
  kubernetes = {
    host                   = kind_cluster.dc.endpoint
    cluster_ca_certificate = kind_cluster.dc.cluster_ca_certificate
    client_certificate     = kind_cluster.dc.client_certificate
    client_key             = kind_cluster.dc.client_key
  }
}

module "stack" {
  source = "./bundle"

  # What identifies the cluster; a change replaces every release. See
  # "Cluster rollover" below.
  cluster_keepers = kind_cluster.dc.cluster_ca_certificate
}
```

Then `terraform init && terraform apply` in the calling configuration.

Regenerate without `--terraform-child-module` to get a standalone root module
that reads a kubeconfig instead.

## When the cluster is in the same configuration

Wiring the provider to a cluster resource, as above, means its attributes are
unknown until the cluster exists. That is fine: `helm_release` does not contact
the API server during planning, so an unknown provider configuration does not
block the plan. One `terraform apply` creates the cluster and installs the
whole bundle behind it.

This is why the bundle is a child module rather than a root module with its own
provider block. A module carrying a provider block cannot take `depends_on`,
`count` or `for_each`, which is exactly what a caller needs to sequence the
bundle behind the cluster that hosts it.

## The dependency graph

`depends_on` on each module call carries the recipe's `dependencyRefs`
**exactly**. A component waits for its declared dependencies and for nothing
else, so independent components apply concurrently.

That is a stronger guarantee than the tier-based deployers can give.
`argocd` projects the graph onto integer sync-waves and `helmfile` onto nested
level files; both are total orders, so a component ends up waiting for every
sibling at the prior depth rather than for its own dependencies. Only `flux`
(`dependsOn`) and this deployer keep the graph.

The edge sits on the module **call**, not on the `helm_release` inside it. A
`depends_on` on a call is a fact about everything the module contains, so the
ordering survives the module growing a second resource.

Components that expand into more than one release — a `-pre` manifest chart, a
`-post` chart, a readiness gate — chain internally, and a dependent waits for
the **last** release in that chain, not just the primary chart.

## What `wait` does and does not buy you

`var.wait` (default `true`) makes each `helm_release` wait for its workloads
to become ready, which is what turns an ordering edge into a readiness edge.

It does **not** wait on custom-resource status. A component whose real signal
is a CR condition — `ClusterPolicy.status.state=ready`,
`NicClusterPolicy.status.state=ready` — will report applied while that
condition is still pending. Regenerate with `--readiness-hooks` to get an
explicit gate: each gated component grows a `-readiness` release whose Job
blocks the dependents until the signal actually passes, and which re-runs
whenever that release is upgraded.

## Cluster rollover

This bundle was generated with `--terraform-cluster-rollover`. Each component
module carries a `terraform_data` keyed on `var.cluster_keepers`, and every
release in it a `replace_triggered_by` on that resource: when the keepers
change, every release is replaced, destroy-then-create, rather than left in
state describing objects in a cluster that no longer exists.

The keepers are your statement of what identifies the cluster, so set them to
attributes that change when it is rebuilt. An API endpoint survives a rebuild
behind a DNS name or a VIP; a cluster name is reused by design; a kubeconfig
context is a local alias. What reliably changes:

| Cluster resource | Keeper |
|---|---|
| `kind_cluster` | `cluster_ca_certificate`, or `endpoint` (a port minted per cluster) |
| `aws_eks_cluster` | `certificate_authority[0].data`, or `created_at` (not `id`, which is the name) |
| `google_container_cluster` | `id`, or `master_auth[0].cluster_ca_certificate` |
| `azurerm_kubernetes_cluster` | `id`, or `kube_config[0].cluster_ca_certificate` |
| any | `{ ca = …, id = … }` — a map combines several |

The variable is required and has no default, so every release is contained
from its first apply; any later change to the value replaces every release.
For a cluster this configuration does not manage, its CA certificate still
identifies it: update the value when the cluster is rebuilt and the releases
are replaced with it. A constant keeps the shim inert instead, and then the
flag buys nothing; regenerate without it.
The value may be unknown at plan time; the rule is "the shim is being
replaced", which the plan knows structurally.

What the plan does with it depends on whether it can still see the releases.
When the keepers change on a cluster the plan can reach — one rebuilt behind a
connection that did not change, or a keeper bumped on purpose to reinstall —
the shim does the work: every release is uninstalled and installed again,
gates re-asserting (measured on Terraform 1.16: `17 will be replaced due to
changes in replace_triggered_by`, 17 uninstalls, then 17 installs). When the
cluster is declared in the same configuration and is itself being replaced,
the provider's configuration is unknown while planning, and `hashicorp/helm`
reports a release it cannot reach as deleted — its `Read` drops the resource
on any failed existence check. That plan creates every release in the new
cluster and uninstalls none in the old one, which is harmless when the old
cluster is destroyed and a set of orphaned releases when it is not; the shim
replaces only itself. Either way the end state is one cluster with every
release in it and a clean plan afterwards.

## Layout

```
main.tf                     # the module calls, and the graph
versions.tf                 # required_providers
variables.tf                # wait/timeout/atomic
outputs.tf
modules/component/          # the shared module every call resolves to; holds the
                            #   component's pre / chart / post / readiness releases
NNN-<component>/            # values.yaml and cluster-values.yaml, plus
                            #   Chart.yaml + templates/ for a bundled chart
```

The `NNN-<component>/` folders are the standard AICR bundle layout, written by
the same code that writes them for `--deployer helm` and `--deployer helmfile`,
without helm's `install.sh` and `upstream.env`: the module call in `main.tf`
carries the chart, repository and version, and there is no second way to
install what Terraform manages.

## Addressing a component

The names in this bundle are a contract, so that tooling outside it can refer
in. A component `foo-bar` is `module.foo_bar` (its name with every character
outside `[A-Za-z0-9_]` replaced by `_`, and prefixed with `_` if it would start
with a digit), and inside it the releases are `helm_release.this` (the chart),
with `helm_release.pre`, `helm_release.post` and `helm_release.readiness` beside
it where the bundle emitted those folders (each `count`ed, so `[0]` when
present). Those are the addresses that `terraform apply -replace`, `-target`,
`terraform state`, `moved` and `import` blocks, and a policy over the plan JSON
use, as in `module.stack.module.gpu_operator.helm_release.this` from a root that
calls this bundle as `module "stack"`. Configuration cannot reach inside a
module call: a `depends_on` or `replace_triggered_by` in the caller names
`module.stack` as a whole, and what the caller reads are this bundle's outputs
(`components`, `releases`, `namespaces`). Regenerating keeps these names.

## Scheduling

Unless the recipe was bundled with `--system-node-toleration` (or a
`scheduling.systemNodeTolerations` block), AICR's component defaults give every
runtime operator `tolerations: [{operator: Exists}]`: it tolerates every taint,
the control plane's and a cordon's included. That is what keeps the runtime
running on a small or a tainted cluster, and it is also why `kubectl drain`
moves the tenant's workloads but not these operators — an evicted operator can
be scheduled straight back onto the cordoned node. A node-maintenance step that
waits for a node to empty should not count pods that tolerate the cordon, or
the recipe should narrow the toleration to the system nodes it means.

## Upgrades and replacements

An upgrade is a regenerated bundle. A bundle is a closed set of files that
`checksums.txt` attests, and `aicr bundle` fails its closed-world check when
the output directory holds anything else, so a bundle is always generated into
a fresh directory.

Generate the new bundle beside this one, with the flags this
one was generated with, and point the calling configuration's `source` at it.
That configuration owns the state, the lock file and the variables, so nothing
else moves:

```sh
aicr bundle --recipe <new recipe> --output ./bundle-next --deployer terraform --terraform-child-module
```

Then `terraform init && terraform plan` in the calling configuration (`init`
picks up the new module source).

Read the diff:

- A chart version or values change on a component plans as an **in-place
  update** of `helm_release.this`: `helm upgrade`, with `wait` and `timeout`
  applied as on install. Its dependents are ordered after it, not changed.
- A readiness gate re-runs on every upgrade of **its own** release: the Job
  is a `post-install,post-upgrade` hook with `hook-delete-policy:
  before-hook-creation`, so Helm deletes the last Job and runs a fresh one.
  A gate whose own inputs did not change plans clean and does not re-run; to
  re-assert a component by hand, `terraform apply
  -replace='module.<label>.helm_release.readiness[0]'`, with the label from
  "Addressing a component" above and the caller's `module.stack.` prefix when
  this bundle is called as a module.
- A chart bundled in this directory — a `-pre`, `-post` or `-readiness`
  folder, a vendored chart, or a local chart from `--data` — is tracked by
  **content**: its module call carries a digest of the folder, recorded as
  the release description (`helm history` shows it), so a regenerated folder
  whose files changed plans as an in-place update even though every bundled
  chart's `Chart.yaml` version is the AICR version that generated it. The
  provider re-reads the directory on that upgrade, and a gate whose folder
  changed re-runs.
- Folder numbers are a serialization of the graph. A recipe that adds a
  component earlier in the order renumbers the folders after it, which
  changes the `chart` path of every bundled chart behind them — an in-place
  update each, and a hook re-run on each gate among them.
- Helm installs a chart's `crds/` once and never upgrades them, and this
  bundle has no CRD step of its own. Before upgrading a component whose CRDs
  changed, apply the new CRDs with the CRD-apply command under "Upgrading
  components that own CRDs" in AICR's component catalog, with `CHART` and
  `VERSION` set to the component's new coordinates, `REPO` for a chart from a
  classic repository, `EXCLUDE_SUBCHARTS` from the registry's
  `ownsCRDsExcludeSubcharts`, and `MANAGER=terraform-provider-helm`, the
  field manager the provider installed the CRDs under (the helm deployer's
  `apply-crds.sh` does the same). `aicr upgrade-check --deployer terraform`
  lists the components that need it. Skipped, the chart's new resources may
  fail validation.

A **replacement** is destroy-then-create. `terraform apply -replace` on a
slot, a changed release name or namespace, or a tainted release uninstalls
and reinstalls it; the reinstall fires `post-install`, so a replaced gate
re-asserts. Dependents stay installed throughout — `depends_on` orders them,
it does not replace them. `terraform destroy` uninstalls every release in
reverse dependency order and, like `helm uninstall`, leaves CRDs in place.
Replacing the **cluster** is the case the containment
shim exists for; see "Cluster rollover" above.

## Editing

`main.tf`, `versions.tf`, `variables.tf`, `outputs.tf`, `modules/component/`
and every `NNN-<component>/` folder are generated, `cluster-values.yaml`
included, and a regenerated bundle is a new directory
(see "Upgrades and replacements"). Per-cluster settings belong in
the calling configuration;
for a `--dynamic` path, fill in the component's
`cluster-values.yaml` after each regeneration, or keep that file under your
own version control and restore it.
